title: SEBI Proposes Mutual Fund-Only PMS Category With Lower Entry Threshold
excerpt: India's market regulator wants to create a dedicated portfolio management service that invests exclusively in mutual funds, cutting the minimum investment to ₹25 lakh from ₹50 lakh.
body:
• SEBI's consultation paper proposes a new MF-only PMS category with a ₹25 lakh minimum investment, half the current ₹50 lakh threshold for regular PMS
  • Portfolio managers under the new framework would invest exclusively in direct plans of mutual funds, ETFs and specialised investment funds
  • The PMS industry has grown to ₹42.61 lakh crore in assets under management with over 515 registered portfolio managers

The Securities and Exchange Board of India has proposed creating a dedicated mutual fund-only portfolio management service category, a move that could open professionally managed portfolios to a broader swath of investors while reshaping the competitive landscape between wealth managers and fund distributors.

The proposal, outlined in a consultation paper dated July 23, seeks to carve out a formal regulatory space for portfolio managers who invest client money exclusively in direct plans of mutual fund schemes, exchange-traded funds and specialised investment funds. Public comments are open until August 13.

What Changes for Investors

The most consequential shift is the entry threshold. Under the proposed MF-PMS framework, the minimum investment drops to ₹25 lakh — half the ₹50 lakh required for any PMS today. The net worth requirement for firms seeking to set up an MF-PMS operation would also fall, to ₹2 crore from ₹5 crore, according to SEBI's paper.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=S4L5BkIuz4U

Fixed management fees would be capped at 2.5 percent of assets under management, with portfolio managers also permitted to charge performance-based fees or a combination of both, subject to client consent. To protect investors from being charged exit loads at both the PMS and mutual fund levels, exit load provisions at the PMS layer will not apply to MF-PMS accounts.

"MF-PMS bridges this gap by allowing the emerging HNI segment to combine the cost advantages of direct mutual funds with the expertise of professional portfolio managers."

— Karan Aggarwal, Co-founder and CIO, Ametra PMS

Industry Divided on Value Proposition

Not everyone in the wealth management industry is convinced the new category fills an unmet need. Bhavin Shah, founder and portfolio manager at Sameeksha Capital and a board member of the Association of Portfolio Managers in India, said the proposal raises questions about differentiation.

"It is not clear what gap it serves because MF-PMS is already possible through the regular PMS route," Shah told The Hindu BusinessLine. He also flagged a structural constraint: SEBI has proposed that the same client cannot be serviced through both the distribution mode and the MF-PMS mode, even if the services are offered by separate divisions within the same firm.

Investors would also bear a dual cost layer — the underlying mutual fund expense ratio plus the PMS management fee — a point that could limit uptake among cost-conscious investors already comfortable with direct mutual fund plans.

A Booming Industry Gets New Rules

The proposed overhaul comes as the PMS industry has entered a period of rapid expansion. Assets under management surged to ₹42.61 lakh crore as of May 2026, up from ₹18.07 lakh crore in April 2019, according to SEBI data. The number of registered portfolio managers more than doubled to 515 from 226 in 2020, when the current PMS regulations were introduced.

Client numbers have also climbed, reaching 2.19 lakh from 1.5 lakh over the same period. SEBI said the review was driven by the industry's significant growth, increasing technology adoption and rising investor demand for personalised solutions.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs and members of the Indian diaspora who maintain investment portfolios in India, the lower entry point could make professionally managed mutual fund portfolios more accessible. The MF-PMS structure — built on direct plans that eliminate distributor commissions — may appeal to overseas investors seeking cost-efficient, discretionary management of their India allocations without meeting the ₹50 lakh minimum that regular PMS currently demands.

What Comes Next

The consultation paper is the first step in what could be a multi-month regulatory process. After public comments close on August 13, SEBI will review feedback before deciding whether to finalise the framework. If approved, existing portfolio managers would be permitted to offer MF-PMS through a separate investment approach under a dedicated registration, potentially expanding the product menu available to India's growing mass-affluent investor base.
